title: Two swords, one circle
told: a sakhi of Guru Hargobind, a traditional story

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? do you ever feel pulled between your busy life and your inner life?
options: then this one is for you. listen.
then you’ll like this answer. listen.
then listen. you might be doing it already.

steps.line: When Guru Hargobind became the sixth Guru, still very young, he asked for not one sword but two.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: One sword stood for miri, life in the world: leading and protecting people. The other for piri, the life of the spirit.

steps.q: Guru Hargobind took up two swords soon after something happened to his father, the fifth Guru. What?
o: His father was killed by the rulers
His father gave up the Guru’s seat
His father won a great battle
steps.why: Guru Arjan died under torture by Mughal authorities in 1606. His young son took up two swords, so the Sikhs would never be defenseless again.

steps.line: Years later, riding with his Sikhs through the hills, he met a famous wandering holy man, Samarth Ramdas.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: The holy man asked: you sit on Guru Nanak’s seat. Why ride with swords and horses?

steps.q: How do you think the Guru answers?
o: I gave up the hermit’s life to defend
These swords are only for show
Inside, a hermit. Outside, a prince.
steps.why: Inside, a hermit. Outside, a prince. Many tellings say the holy man was satisfied with that.

steps.line: Inside, a hermit, the Guru said. Outside, a prince. The sword is to protect the poor and stand up to cruelty.

steps.q: Guru Hargobind also built a second seat, facing the Golden Temple. What was it for?
o: Training young Sikh soldiers to ride
Ruling on the Sikhs’ worldly affairs
Housing a shrine to his father
steps.why: The Akal Takht, throne of the Timeless, faces the Harmandir Sahib: the world and the spirit side by side. It still guides Sikhs today.

steps.q: Those two swords live on in a famous symbol. Where do you think it is?
steps.why: On the Nishan Sahib, the Sikh flag that flies at gurdwaras.

steps.line: Today two curved swords wrap around the Khanda, the symbol on the Sikh flag: a circle, and a double-edged sword in the middle.
steps.label: today

steps.line: The circle has no beginning and no end, like the one God. The middle sword cuts truth from lies. The two outside: world and spirit, held together.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Initiated Sikhs carry a small sword, the kirpan. Many say the word joins two ideas. Which?
steps.why: Many explain kirpan as kirpa, mercy, and aan, honor: a sword for protecting, never for attacking.

say: here’s what i love. the guru didn’t choose between a holy life and a busy one. he carried both.
that’s the khanda on the sikh flag: truth in the middle, the one god all around, and world and spirit held together.

steps.q: The holy man thought swords didn’t belong on Guru Nanak’s seat. From the answer, did Guru Hargobind leave Guru Nanak’s path?
o: Yes, he traded prayer for power
No: same inner life, plus a duty to protect
Yes, he left the spirit to holy men
steps.why: No. Inside, the same hermit’s heart. Outside, a prince’s duty to the poor. Miri and piri, held together.

today.say: today, in the middle of your busiest hour, pause for one breath and, if you like, say waheguru inside. then go right back to work. a sikh keeps both: honest work and remembering god.
options: inside a hermit, outside a prince. that’s the breath.
i hear you. then that’s exactly the hour. just one breath.

tomorrow.line: a whole week done. next, the kitchen, and the people you never notice.

sources: Sikh tradition of Guru Hargobind wearing two swords, miri and piri, at his installation as Guru (1606)

Meeting of Guru Hargobind and Samarth Ramdas, as recorded in the Pothi Panjah Sakhian; the reply “batan faqiri, zahir amiri, shastar garib ki rakhya, jarwane ki bhakhya” (inwardly a hermit, outwardly a prince; arms to protect the poor and resist the tyrant)
The Khanda emblem and the Nishan Sahib
check: The Samarth Ramdas meeting comes from a later source (Panjah Sakhian) and its historicity is debated; it is labeled “a traditional story”.

Reading of the middle sword as cutting truth from lies, and the circle as the one without end, follow common Sikh explanation; the emblem’s current standard form is fairly modern; confirm framing of the two curved swords as miri and piri.
